newsitem.title: MALAWI: Weather smiles on impoverished Malawi economy.
newsitem.headline: Weather smiles on impoverished Malawi economy.

text.p: Good rains over the last three years have pushed economic growth in Malawi and the government is confident of another year of above-average expansion.

Real gross domestic product (GDP) in the agriculture-based southern Africa country.grew by 9.5 percent in 1996, after nine percent in 1995, far outstripping Africa's average growth in 1996 of five percent, according to Finance Minister Aleke Banda.

The government's latest official report on the economy says growth will moderate somewhat in 1997 to 7.1 percent, but all sectors are expected to perform well. Agricultural output is expected to grow by 5.7 percent in 1997.
Total exports are predicted to grow from 6.7 billion kwacha ($440 million) in 1996 to 7.7 billion in 1997.
"It is expected that the favourable and steady exchange rate regime will help exporters to take up the export drive in 1997," the report says.
Malawi's currency, the kwacha, currently sells at 15.21 to a dollar, a level it has broadly maintained for well over a year.
Tobacco will once again be the main driver of exports, with production climbing following favourable weather and the liberalisation of agricultural marketing.
Tobacco sales last year generated 4.2 billion kwacha, which represented more than 60 percent of total exports.
Since 1995 Malawi has adopted comprehensive economic restructuring measures, helped by loans from the International Monetary Fund under an enhanced structural adjustment facility.
The reforms, including moves to cut the budget deficit, are already bearing fruit with annual inflation down to 7.1 percent by March this year, compared to 73.9 percent a year ago.
The official discount rate stands at 27 percent compared to 50 percent one year ago.

Analysts say the outlook is improving for a country which ranks among the poorest in the world with average gross national product (GNP) per capita of just $170, according to the World Bank's 1996 Development Report.
But further positive growth will be weather-dependent and infrastructure development remains precarious.
At least 500,000 potential subscribers have been waiting for the last three years to be connected to the state-run telephone network.
And although more than 1,000 mobile telephones have been sold by Telekom Malaysia in partnership with the Malawi government, the price is too high for the average citizen.
The 15,000-km tarred road network has also been crippled by potholes which Malawians nickname "bath tubs". Most have not been repaired in the last 30 years.
